claims.claim_text: For a fixed function, a dedicated embedded processor will generally beat an FPGA on power consumption, which is why low-power claims from FPGA vendors are only meaningful relative to other FPGAs.
claims.quote_verbatim: You're always going to get a lower power solution in a, you know, a dedicated embedded processor
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Critical Mass

claims.claim_text: FPGA and microcontroller vendor toolchains have historically shipped as a single monolithic install covering every supported device and board support package rather than downloading on demand, because one daily build of one package is easier for the vendor to manage than a hundred separately versioned downloads.
claims.quote_verbatim: there's, like, this archaic system where they pull every single chip that's available, every board support package, all in at the same time
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: LED Designs, Last Minute Designs and Board Designs

claims.claim_text: In low-volume products engineering time dominates bill-of-materials cost, so designers will accept a three-hundred-dollar FPGA and its vendor reference design rather than spend weeks optimising down to a cheaper part.
claims.quote_verbatim: they have no problem throwing in a $300 FPGA
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: OSHW, Makerbot & Memristo - Maundering Memristor Mathematicaster

claims.claim_text: Because an FPGA's function lives in a reloadable bitstream, a contentious or licence-encumbered feature can be removed from an already-manufactured product without any hardware change, and the same board resold with a different personality.
claims.quote_verbatim: the nice thing about using FPGA is I can say, okay, well, you know what? The thing you didn't like, it's gone.
claims.speaker: Bunnie Huang
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Bunnie Huang - Bunnie's Bibelot Bonification

claims.claim_text: Where the end user is expected to modify the FPGA fabric, the vendor choice is dictated by the toolchain the user already knows rather than by the silicon; a closed product whose fabric the customer never touches leaves the designer free to pick on price and pinout.
claims.quote_verbatim: since my users want to modify the FPGA and they want to do it in tools they're familiar with, I need to give them the Xilinx chip that they're expecting
claims.speaker: Matt Ettus
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Matt Ettus - Quality Quadrature Quidam

claims.claim_text: Pin count, not logic capacity, is what pushes a design out of the low-cost FPGA families: a modular radio whose daughterboard interface consumed about 110 pins could not support two such slots, since 220 pins is difficult to obtain in a low-cost part.
claims.quote_verbatim: Each of our daughter board interfaces today takes, takes, I think it's about 110 pins. You put two on there, you now need 220 pins and it's a lot harder to get that in a low cost FPGA.
claims.speaker: Matt Ettus
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Matt Ettus - Quality Quadrature Quidam

claims.claim_text: The FPGA and the microcontroller converged from both directions: FPGAs gained hard silicon processors and peripherals, while microcontrollers gained small blocks of embedded programmable fabric, blurring the boundary between the two device classes.
claims.quote_verbatim: The FPGAs now have hard silicon on them to do the, you know, to do the microcontroller type stuff.
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Gouging Green Gardyloo

claims.claim_text: Xilinx's early product line ran from the 2000 series, which comprised two part numbers, through the 3000 series topped by the 3090, to the 4000 series, whose architecture was still being defined at the end of the 1980s with the lookup tables and flip-flops settled and the carry logic still under argument.
claims.quote_verbatim: The last of the 3000 series was just going out the door. So, that was the 3090.
claims.speaker: Philip Frieden
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Philip Freidin - Xenodochial Xilinx Ex-Employee

claims.claim_text: The routing architecture, not the logic cell, is the dominant design decision in an FPGA and set the competitive position of Xilinx's parts for more than fifteen years after the 4000 series.
claims.quote_verbatim: much more important than anything else on an FPGA for the next 15 plus years was how do we do the routing
claims.speaker: Philip Frieden
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Philip Freidin - Xenodochial Xilinx Ex-Employee

claims.claim_text: The price of an FPGA tracks the sheer size of its die rather than any premium for programmability; per unit of silicon delivered, FPGAs are not priced differently from other chips.
claims.quote_verbatim: So the price of FPGAs is the sheer size of the die, basically.
claims.speaker: Philip Frieden
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Philip Freidin - Xenodochial Xilinx Ex-Employee

claims.claim_text: FPGA vendors price on the same model as other semiconductor makers: gross margins at Xilinx and Intel sat within a few percent of each other, so the perception that FPGAs carry an exceptional markup reflects die size rather than pricing policy.
claims.quote_verbatim: If you look at the gross margin for Xilinx versus, say, gross margin for Intel, they're within a few percent of each other.
claims.speaker: Philip Frieden
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Philip Freidin - Xenodochial Xilinx Ex-Employee

claims.claim_text: An FPGA and a microcontroller occupy different market segments rather than competing: a ten-dollar FPGA maps an unlimited variety of designs, but where a fifty-cent microcontroller suffices the FPGA is the wrong tool.
claims.quote_verbatim: It's a $10 part. Whereas if you just need your 50 cent micro, then an FPGA is not, you know, is not the solution for you.
claims.speaker: Philip Frieden
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Philip Freidin - Xenodochial Xilinx Ex-Employee

claims.claim_text: The task that separates the FPGA from the processor is concurrent real-time observation: watching three lines toggling at 10 MHz and extracting a bit pattern on the fly is beyond any single processor, and is routine for a ten-dollar FPGA.
claims.quote_verbatim: if you have to watch three signal lines that are toggling at 10 megahertz, right, and pull out a bit pattern on the fly, there isn't a processor on the market that can do that
claims.speaker: Philip Frieden
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Philip Freidin - Xenodochial Xilinx Ex-Employee

claims.claim_text: Instantiating a soft CPU core in an FPGA and running ordinary sequential code on it duplicates what a microcontroller already does and uses none of the fabric's advantages; the fabric earns its cost only where concurrency or determinism is required.
claims.quote_verbatim: They're just duplicating what a micro controller does
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Philip Freidin - Xenodochial Xilinx Ex-Employee

claims.claim_text: FPGAs displace ASICs not by being intrinsically better but because fabs move relentlessly to tighter geometries on larger wafers, driving mask-set cost for a leading-edge process past ten million dollars and shrinking the volume band in which an ASIC pays back.
claims.quote_verbatim: we're now talking about mask sets for chips that are using the most current technology getting over $10 million for a mask set
claims.speaker: Philip Frieden
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Philip Freidin - Xenodochial Xilinx Ex-Employee

claims.claim_text: For roughly 95 percent of designs likely to end up in an FPGA, a design working on one vendor's part can be made to work on another's; vendor lock-in comes from tools, IP blocks and habit rather than from the fabric itself.
claims.quote_verbatim: for 95% of all designs that are likely to end up inside an FPGA, if you can get it to work in one vendor's product, you can get it to work in the other guy's product
claims.speaker: Philip Frieden
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Philip Freidin - Xenodochial Xilinx Ex-Employee

claims.claim_text: FPGAs present a steeper entry barrier than microcontrollers because almost every electronics engineer already programs in C, while hardware description languages demand an unfamiliar concurrent paradigm.
claims.quote_verbatim: every electronics engineer knows how to program in C, right? Just, you know, and use microcontrollers. It's natural to them.
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: Tektronix, ChipReport.tv, & the Signal Path - Temperative Tegmen Temperature

claims.claim_text: Digital beamforming for phased-array radar and sonar, where many antenna elements are combined to steer a beam electronically instead of mechanically, is a traditional application for top-end FPGAs costing around ten thousand dollars each.
claims.quote_verbatim: beamforming is one of your traditional uses for the year ten thousand dollar high-end fpga chips
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Dr Greg Charvat - Watcher of Wraithlike Walls

claims.claim_text: The parallel nature of logic in an FPGA, where everything happens at once, is harder to internalise than sequential line-by-line execution, and the difficulty is compounded because most engineers and hobbyists arrive with some prior sequential programming experience to unlearn.
claims.quote_verbatim: I think as a general rule, the parallel processing nature of the FPGA is harder to understand, is a more difficult concept to understand than line by line
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: FPGA, Xess, 32 Bit - Quirky Qualitative Questions

claims.claim_text: A commercial reconfigurable I/O platform partitions its FPGA into fixed vendor IP for the bus interface and DRAM, a window for the user's high-level code, and a second window for low-level logic that talks to the user's circuit; a module developer kit documents the timing and mechanical constraints for that second window.
claims.quote_verbatim: the FPGA has fixed IP for the, the bus interface, the DRAM, the things that are always there
claims.speaker: Ryan Brown
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Ryan Brown - Effortless Equipment Extensibility

claims.claim_text: The reliable way into FPGA work is to buy a development board with a working example, get that example running, and then work backwards into how the configuration and toolchain actually operate.
claims.quote_verbatim: The universal answer to starting with FPGAs, and it's very similar for micros and everything else, is start with a working example.
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: FPGAs, Robots & Thermocouples - Wampum's Wavering Worth

claims.claim_text: A metallised gate array sits between the FPGA and the full custom ASIC: the base wafer is common and only the metal layers are customised, which cuts non-recurring engineering cost relative to a full mask set while removing the FPGA's reconfigurability.
claims.quote_verbatim: it's not a full ASIC. It's a gate array
claims.speaker: Jeri Ellsworth
claims.episode_title: An interview with Jeri Ellsworth - Absorptive Augmented Actuality

claims.claim_text: A design intended for custom silicon is normally proven first in an FPGA, so the risk in an ASIC programme is any block with no FPGA equivalent; high-speed serialisers are the usual gap, leaving properties such as trace-length tolerance untestable before tape-out.
claims.quote_verbatim: the only thing I have anxiety about right now is the serializers that I'm not going to be able to find something that's equivalent in an FPGA so I can actually test wire length
claims.speaker: Jeri Ellsworth
claims.episode_title: An interview with Jeri Ellsworth - Absorptive Augmented Actuality

claims.claim_text: Migrating a design from FPGA to ASIC forfeits reconfigurability, so a common mitigation is to embed a small soft processor core in the ASIC to handle housekeeping in otherwise idle intervals, keeping behaviour changeable in firmware rather than frozen in silicon.
claims.quote_verbatim: That's why we have that little 6502 hanging out in there that does a bunch of stuff in the blanking period. That way we don't hard code anything.
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: An interview with Jeri Ellsworth - Absorptive Augmented Actuality

claims.claim_text: All four major FPGA vendors reintroduced hard processor cores into their fabric, an admission that pure programmable logic was not displacing the processor and that customers wanted conventional sequential compute alongside it.
claims.quote_verbatim: I think every top, all the top four vendors have that now where they all have a hard processor in there again
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: Solar, FPGAs and Maxim Integrated - Solar Shopper Sickness

claims.claim_text: On an FPGA system-on-chip such as the Zynq, the hard peripheral set of USB, gigabit Ethernet, SDIO, UART, CAN, I2C and SPI could all be implemented in fabric instead; the analogue-to-digital converters are the part that cannot, which is why hardening the digital peripherals buys area and power rather than capability.
claims.quote_verbatim: aside from the analog to digital converters, all of those things are possible in Fabric anyways because it's just an FPGA
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: Tesla, FPGAs and DigiKey - Zesty Zippy Zynq

claims.claim_text: Verilog reached FPGA design around the mid-1990s, arriving from custom silicon design where it was already established; before that FPGA designs were entered as schematics, and schematic entry has remained available in vendor tools since.
claims.quote_verbatim: at the time for FPGAs, Verilog was new because everybody at that time was still either doing schematic entry
claims.speaker: Vincent Himpe
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Vincent Himpe - Escaped Electron Elocution

claims.claim_text: The choice of soft processor core is constrained by architecture licensing rather than by technology: Intel treated its 8048 and 8051 as end-of-life standard products and tolerated hundreds of clones, while Motorola, Microchip and Atmel defended their cores, which is why open cores cluster around the former.
claims.quote_verbatim: The 8051 has been cloned to death by over 300 companies.
claims.speaker: Vincent Himpe
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Vincent Himpe - Escaped Electron Elocution

claims.claim_text: ASIC verification uses hardware emulation boxes containing grids of high-end FPGAs that implement the chip under design, so that the design runs at a usable speed instead of being software-simulated.
claims.quote_verbatim: they have just these farms of FPGAs that are used to simulate in hardware, simulate ASIC designs
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Funding New/Manufacturing Old Projects - Radical Robotic Requisition

claims.claim_text: The structural advantage of an FPGA over a processor is streaming: data can be processed as it arrives at full rate, rather than buffered into a block and post-processed by iteration.
claims.quote_verbatim: If you're streaming through an FPGA, you can do a lot more samples in a shorter amount of time versus having to take a big chunk of data and then iterate on it.
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: A 2013 Recap - Year-end Yarn Yakking

claims.claim_text: Intel made FPGAs in the early 1990s, exited, and re-entered the market decades later, so its present position in programmable logic is a return rather than a first entry.
claims.quote_verbatim: Did you guys know that Intel used to make FPGAs?
claims.speaker: Dave Vandenbout
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Dave Vandenbout - Xceptional XESS Xenagogue

claims.claim_text: The screening question for an FPGA is bandwidth and concurrency: human-interaction and other low-bandwidth tasks belong on a microcontroller, and the fabric is justified only where there are genuinely parallel processes or hard latency requirements.
claims.quote_verbatim: if you've got something where you need a lot of, where you have parallel processes and a lot of fast latency that you have to worry about, then you can start looking at FPGA
claims.speaker: Dave Vandenbout
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Dave Vandenbout - Xceptional XESS Xenagogue

claims.claim_text: A development-board vendor moves to a new FPGA generation when three things line up: density has risen to what customers expect, price has fallen far enough to be viable, and supply is available without competing for allocation against much larger customers.
claims.quote_verbatim: when I switch from one iteration to the next, it's mainly that the density has gotten up to the point where people are starting to expect it
claims.speaker: Dave Vandenbout
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Dave Vandenbout - Xceptional XESS Xenagogue

claims.claim_text: MyHDL is a Python library for logic design rather than a separate language, which allows a design to be described, simulated and manipulated with ordinary Python tooling.
claims.quote_verbatim: It's, you know, it's just a Python library that you can, you know, load up and do logic design with it.
claims.speaker: Dave Vandenbout
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Dave Vandenbout - Xceptional XESS Xenagogue

claims.claim_text: The dominant cost in learning an FPGA toolchain is procedural rather than conceptual: vendor tutorials run to dozens of pages of screenshots before a first LED blinks, because every dialogue in the flow has to be shown.
claims.quote_verbatim: I had to go through 80 pages in this book to, you know, get an LED to blink
claims.speaker: Dave Vandenbout
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Dave Vandenbout - Xceptional XESS Xenagogue

claims.claim_text: A USB core implemented in fabric consumes on the order of ten thousand logic elements, which rules out the smallest one-dollar FPGAs and puts the design in a mid-range part costing five to ten dollars before any of the application logic is added.
claims.quote_verbatim: it's something on the order of like, uh, 10,000 logic elements for the USB core
claims.speaker: Michael Ossmann
claims.episode_title: Mike Ossmann Returns! - Planetic Portalab Packaging

claims.claim_text: A general-purpose FPGA carrier board reduces to an FPGA, a host interface, a memory socket and a mezzanine connector, with only power supplies, a clock generator and a small supervisory microcontroller besides; application-specific analogue front ends then arrive as plug-in daughterboards.
claims.quote_verbatim: So basically the main board is an FPGA, the USB 3.0 interface, a big mezzanine connector
claims.speaker: Michael Ossmann
claims.episode_title: Mike Ossmann Returns! - Planetic Portalab Packaging

claims.claim_text: Selecting an FPGA for a pin-limited design reduces to a parametric search sorted by pin count and then by price, and frequently lands one generation behind the current family, since the newest family often has no part offering that pin count at the lower price point.
claims.quote_verbatim: there's no part in the Cyclone 5 family that has this many pins for that lower cost
claims.speaker: Michael Ossmann
claims.episode_title: Mike Ossmann Returns! - Planetic Portalab Packaging

claims.claim_text: A wideband software-defined radio designed to run from a USB 2.0 port met its cost and power budget by omitting the FPGA entirely: a small CPLD provides glue logic such as unsigned-to-signed conversion, and an ARM Cortex-M4 with DSP instructions does the processing.
claims.quote_verbatim: one way I was able to reduce costs and power consumption is just to go without an FPGA. There is a small CPLD on it.
claims.speaker: Michael Ossmann
claims.episode_title: Impedance Matching With Charvat And Ossmann - Recurring RF Remontados

claims.claim_text: A radio-astronomy and phased-array radar group fielding systems on a twelve to eighteen month cycle adopted an unofficial policy of no longer using FPGAs, because the development and debug time the fabric demands does not fit that schedule.
claims.quote_verbatim: their unofficial policy is to no longer use FPGAs
claims.speaker: Greg Charvat
claims.episode_title: Impedance Matching With Charvat And Ossmann - Recurring RF Remontados

claims.claim_text: Partitioning a system so that safety interlocks live in fixed FPGA logic in the backplane, while all user code runs on the processor, keeps the safety-critical behaviour outside the reach of the application programmer.
claims.quote_verbatim: there's an FPGA in the backplane that handles safety stuff and everything that the students don't need to be wondering about
claims.speaker: Eric Van Wyk
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Eric VanWyk - Meiotic Mountenance Mooshimeter

claims.claim_text: Altera's Max branding, long associated with CPLDs such as the Max 3000, was reused for the Max 10 low-cost FPGA even though the Max parts had used FPGA fabric internally for some time, so the family name is a poor guide to the device architecture.
claims.quote_verbatim: they've decided to call their new low-cost one the Max 10 instead of calling it the Cyclone 20
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Get Smart About Automation - Caducous Cyborg Concerns

claims.claim_text: Porting an existing processor design into an FPGA reproduces only the digital side: analogue pin functions and other mixed-signal blocks have no equivalent in most fabrics, so an open-sourced chip cannot simply be re-instantiated whole.
claims.quote_verbatim: if you have, like, an analog pin there, you can't do that on most FPGAs
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: Get Smart About Automation - Caducous Cyborg Concerns

claims.claim_text: The Lattice MachXO family is favoured for small designs because it integrates configuration flash, a voltage regulator and an oscillator on chip, removing the external configuration memory, supply rails and clock source that a conventional SRAM-based FPGA requires.
claims.quote_verbatim: FPGA Lattice Mac XO because it's got on-chip flash, on-chip regulator, and on-chip oscillator, reasonable range of sizes.
claims.speaker: Mike Harrison
claims.episode_title: Meracious Mike Manuduction

claims.claim_text: Small-package FPGA options are frequently feature-reduced rather than merely pin-reduced: the 32-pin QFN MachXO omits memory blocks and PLLs entirely, so a design needing either must move to the 100-pin package.
claims.quote_verbatim: They do a 32-pin QFN version, which unfortunately doesn't have any memory blocks or PLLs, and you have to go to 100-pin.
claims.speaker: Mike Harrison
claims.episode_title: Meracious Mike Manuduction

claims.claim_text: Authenticating a product by having its FPGA bitstream challenge the host is defeated by users writing a substitute bitstream that implements the protocol, so a device whose configuration is loaded at run time cannot root its authentication in that configuration.
claims.quote_verbatim: what we actually found, um, people ended up doing is writing their own FPGA bit stream
claims.speaker: Joe Garrison
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Joe and Mark Garrison - Subtly Spelling SayLeeAy

claims.claim_text: When a custom ASIC goes end-of-life, a standard route is to respin the board with an FPGA that replicates the obsolete part's behaviour, which turns an obsolescence problem into a bounded logic-design problem against the old part's observable interface.
claims.quote_verbatim: maybe then you'll go drop an FPGA in there because you have to try and replicate the former ASIC
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: Consolidate All The Things - Zonked Zelotic Zaitech

claims.claim_text: For a fixed function such as a turbo decoder, implementing it in an ASIC rather than an FPGA yields roughly a twenty-fold efficiency advantage or better; ASICs always win technically and lose only because the volume needed to amortise a spin is rarely there.
claims.quote_verbatim: if you put that in FPGA versus making an ASIC for that, you're probably talking about 20x
claims.speaker: Andreas Olofsson
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Andreas Olofsson - Adapteva's Ampliative Abacus

claims.claim_text: A tiled processor architecture can be verified in an FPGA far smaller than the target chip by instantiating only a few tiles: four tiles of a sixteen-core design fitted in a modest part and flushed out almost all the bugs before tape-out.
claims.quote_verbatim: It did flush out almost all the bugs
claims.speaker: Andreas Olofsson
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Andreas Olofsson - Adapteva's Ampliative Abacus

claims.claim_text: For bit-level workloads such as password cracking, which consist of XOR and shuffling operations and need no 32-bit arithmetic, the FPGA fabric of a Zynq outperformed a dedicated many-core floating-point processor on the same board.
claims.quote_verbatim: the zinc was actually the, the winner over the epiphany even
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Andreas Olofsson - Adapteva's Ampliative Abacus

claims.claim_text: Vendor and third-party Simulink blocksets let a non-HDL engineer assemble a math model and emit VHDL or Verilog automatically; the generated code works but is not maintainable as source, so the model rather than the HDL becomes the artefact under version control.
claims.quote_verbatim: you drop, like, these FPGA blocks into Simulink, and then you could basically create, like, these math models, and then, you know, tweak it, and then it would just basically spit out VHDL at Verilog, which is great for an idiot like me. Not great for making maintainable code
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: The Cost Of Doing Business

claims.claim_text: Package availability, not silicon capability, is the long-standing barrier for small-scale FPGA users: the established vendors have little reason to offer hand-solderable packages, so new entrants targeting the low end are the usual source of accessible parts.
claims.quote_verbatim: I've been fighting for more accessible FPGA packages for 20 years
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: The Cost Of Doing Business

claims.claim_text: New FPGA companies have historically mostly failed, because competing with the incumbents requires simultaneously matching silicon, toolchain and IP ecosystem; entrants that survive do so by opening a segment the incumbents do not serve rather than by competing head-on.
claims.quote_verbatim: It's just the history of FPGA shows, FPGA startups, you know, coming into the market just ultimately mostly fail
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: The Cost Of Doing Business

claims.claim_text: Comparing an FPGA against an ASIC on unit price alone is a mistake: die area, physical package size and above all power consumption also separate them, which is why FPGAs rarely reach consumer products even when the price gap closes.
claims.quote_verbatim: Don't make the mistake of trying to compare FPGAs with ASICs. It's not only about price. It's also about area and physical size and, most critically, power consumption as well.
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: The Cost Of Doing Business

claims.claim_text: Whether a die is core-limited or pad-limited explains the FPGA product mix: a logic-rich part is core-limited, so its I/O pads come essentially free with the area already spent on fabric, and vendors long had little incentive to offer high-density parts in low pin-count packages.
claims.quote_verbatim: when you're designing a chip, you're either core limited or pad limited. Meaning that those logic elements inside the die itself dominate the die area or the pads do.
claims.speaker: Luke Beno
claims.episode_title: An Interview With Luke Beno of Analog.io

claims.claim_text: SRAM-based FPGAs are volatile and reload their configuration at every power-up from an external flash device, so the bitstream is exposed on the board and securing the design becomes a question of protecting that transfer rather than the chip alone.
claims.quote_verbatim: security of how do you securely use field programmable gate arrays that are volatile
claims.speaker: Saar Drimer
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Saar Drimer

claims.claim_text: For someone entering accelerated computing, a GPU has a much lower upfront cost than an FPGA solution, so the FPGA route pays back only for workloads run long enough for its power and throughput advantage to dominate the initial outlay.
claims.quote_verbatim: the upfront cost of a GPU is probably much lower than an FPGA solution
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: Gotta Update My Dog

claims.claim_text: Even inexpensive FPGAs deliver very large speed-ups on applications that parallelise across a signal chain, such as video processing and simultaneous acquisition from many sensor inputs.
claims.quote_verbatim: with relatively cheap FPGAs, you can get just almost unbelievable performance increases for certain applications like video processing and, you know, multi-broad sensor inputs
claims.speaker: Clint Cole
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Clint Cole of Digilent

claims.claim_text: FPGA vendors give away the tools for the bulk of their catalogue and charge only for support of the extreme high-end parts, on the reasoning that the designers using five- and ten-thousand-dollar devices are not price-sensitive about tooling.
claims.quote_verbatim: your average Joe is not going to use a $5,000, $10,000 FPGA in their new Internet of Things widget
claims.speaker: Clint Cole
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Clint Cole of Digilent

claims.claim_text: Modern FPGA fabric contains hard arithmetic blocks, including 36-bit multipliers settling in about three nanoseconds, so DSP throughput comes from dedicated silicon within the part rather than from logic built out of lookup tables.
claims.quote_verbatim: things like 36-bit multipliers that converge in three nanoseconds
claims.speaker: Clint Cole
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Clint Cole of Digilent

claims.claim_text: The rising capability of microcontrollers is what keeps FPGAs niche: each generation of processor absorbs applications that would once have needed fabric, so the remaining FPGA territory is only what a processor genuinely cannot do.
claims.quote_verbatim: they're too niche app requirement because micros are so ridiculously powerful that it sort of pushes FPGA into the niche
claims.speaker: Clint Cole
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Clint Cole of Digilent

claims.claim_text: The standard architecture for a high-bandwidth sensor system puts an FPGA in front of the processor to detect features, parameterise them and emit a reduced data stream, so that the processor only ever sees a bandwidth it can handle.
claims.quote_verbatim: you'd have to have something like an FPGA to do all the pre-processing and, you know, find the abrupt transitions and somehow parameterize them, you know, and feed that in a meaningful data stream back to a processor that could handle a reduced bandwidth
claims.speaker: Clint Cole
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Clint Cole of Digilent

claims.claim_text: Games console security has been broken by wiring an FPGA directly to the DRAM lines and corrupting data as the CPU cache is flushed back to memory, an attack that requires logic fast and deterministic enough to act within the memory timing window.
claims.quote_verbatim: they were corrupting the data getting written back to the DRAM by taking an FPGA and interfacing to the DRAM lines
claims.speaker: Dmitry Nedospasov
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Dmitry Nedospasov

claims.claim_text: Microsoft's Project Catapult placed an FPGA in the network path of each Azure server so that all traffic passes from the processor through the fabric before reaching the network, initially doing nothing but pass data through and later reconfigured remotely for hardware acceleration.
claims.quote_verbatim: Instead of just hooking the processor in the server directly onto the, you know, directly onto the internet, we'll put an FPGA in between.
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: A Decoupled Episode

claims.claim_text: Offloading server tasks to an in-path FPGA produced speed-ups reported between ten and a thousand times depending on the task, typically in the low tens.
claims.quote_verbatim: you can get speed increases depending on the task, of course, anywhere from 10 to 1,000 times
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: A Decoupled Episode

claims.claim_text: Remotely reconfigurable fabric across a fleet carries fleet-wide risk: a faulty bitstream pushed to a hundred thousand servers fails everywhere at once, so the deployment discipline has to match that of firmware rather than of application software.
claims.quote_verbatim: if you don't get that logic right and you push out that change to your 100,000 servers
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: A Decoupled Episode

claims.claim_text: Altera promoted a C-to-hardware flow in which the developer wrote C for a soft processor core inside the FPGA, then selected a routine and had the tool synthesise equivalent hardware for it, turning a subroutine call into a hardware accelerator.
claims.quote_verbatim: they used to push this thing where they would do the C to H
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: A Decoupled Episode

claims.claim_text: Commercial bus analysers are built to emit well-formed traffic, which makes them useless for security testing; building the analyser in FPGA fabric is what allows deliberately malformed packets, such as ones whose length field disagrees with the byte count, to be transmitted.
claims.quote_verbatim: if you want to do security analysis, then you actually want to potentially send packets that are in some way malformed or wrong or where the number of bytes doesn't actually match what's in the packet
claims.speaker: Dmitry Nedospasov
claims.episode_title: Impedance Matching with Michael Ossmann and Dmitry Nedospazov

claims.claim_text: Decoding a proprietary or encrypted bus in real time at line rate is not achievable in software on a general-purpose processor, which is what forces the analyser into fabric.
claims.quote_verbatim: if you want to decode the data in real time, you're pretty much screwed unless you're going to use something like an FPGA
claims.speaker: Dmitry Nedospasov
claims.episode_title: Impedance Matching with Michael Ossmann and Dmitry Nedospazov

claims.claim_text: A USB 3.0 man-in-the-middle probe requires the traffic to be passed through fabric at full SuperSpeed rate, which meant developing an open-source USB 3.0 device core in Verilog rather than using a hard controller.
claims.quote_verbatim: we actually implemented USB 3.0 man in the middle running through an FPGA. And we developed an open source USB 3.0 super speed device core.
claims.speaker: Michael Ossmann
claims.episode_title: Impedance Matching with Michael Ossmann and Dmitry Nedospazov

claims.claim_text: A sensor emitting a 1.5 gigabit per second serial stream is commonly deserialised by a small FPGA or CPLD placed next to it, converting the high-rate serial data into a parallel bus a processor can accept.
claims.quote_verbatim: you whack that into a little FPGA or CPLD or something so that you can paralyze it, parallelize it
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Mapping Out Nerdery

claims.claim_text: Putting an FPGA in a product to allow later fixes in HDL only pays off if the deployed units can actually be updated; without a working field-update path the reconfigurability is cost without benefit.
claims.quote_verbatim: you also have to hope that your, your users can change the firmware
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Fake it till you make it

claims.claim_text: A large FPGA can require upwards of a hundred decoupling capacitors, which is the case that motivates scripted or automated capacitor placement in layout tools.
claims.quote_verbatim: Especially for FPGAs when you have, you know, you have sometimes upward, like 100 decoupling caps
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: Fake it till you make it

claims.claim_text: Coarse-grained reconfigurable architectures generalise the FPGA by making the primitive cell operate on whole words rather than single bits, so a single cell can perform an operation such as taking the absolute difference of two numbers and comparing it against a threshold.
claims.quote_verbatim: think of it like, of like an FPGA, but instead of operating on single bits, it is operating on whole worlds and that can do operations like addition and subtraction and multiplication
claims.speaker: Claire Wolf
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Claire (née 'Clifford') Wolf

claims.claim_text: Logic synthesis transforms an HDL description into whatever primitives the target architecture provides: an adder in source becomes a dedicated adder primitive on a coarse-grained array, a carry chain on an FPGA, or NAND and NOR gates for an ASIC. The tool is a compiler in the same sense as a language compiler, bridging a higher-level description to an implementable representation.
claims.quote_verbatim: It might turn that into a chain of carry cells in an FPGA-based synthesis approach. It might turn it into NAND gates and NOR gates for an ASIC synthesis task.
claims.speaker: Claire Wolf
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Claire (née 'Clifford') Wolf

claims.claim_text: The PicoRV32 soft processor occupies roughly 750 lookup tables on Xilinx 7-series fabric and is optimised for very high clock frequency rather than instructions per cycle, taking several cycles per instruction; the point of that trade is that it can share a clock domain with the surrounding high-speed logic and avoid a clock-domain crossing.
claims.quote_verbatim: in Xilinx seven series FPGA architectures, it's about 750 lookup tables large
claims.speaker: Claire Wolf
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Claire (née 'Clifford') Wolf

claims.claim_text: Processor verification departments implement the design in an FPGA and run it continuously for weeks, because failures that only appear after days of running a particular program are not reachable by software simulation.
claims.quote_verbatim: they will implement your processor design in an FPGA and just run it for weeks
claims.speaker: Claire Wolf
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Claire (née 'Clifford') Wolf

claims.claim_text: A host-side bridge onto the FPGA's internal wishbone bus lets scripts on a development machine read and write the registers of peripherals inside the fabric; because the same register API is presented to a soft core running inside the part, a script developed on the host runs unchanged once the bridge is removed.
claims.quote_verbatim: we have these, um, what we call bridges that allow you to, on your host computer, talk to the, um, wishbone bus that connects everything together inside the FPGA
claims.speaker: Tim Ansell
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Tim "Mithro" Ansell

claims.claim_text: Signal processing in a software-defined radio's FPGA runs at very high sample rates using fixed-point integer arithmetic, which introduces small rounding errors that are invisible in most applications and become significant in demanding ones.
claims.quote_verbatim: usually at very high sample rates and so most of that ends up being uh integer uh fixed width mathematics
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Derek Kozel

claims.claim_text: Publishing the FPGA source for a software-defined radio lets users insert their own processing into the signal path to obtain hardware acceleration, and integrating at that level is a distinct capability from the software API.
claims.quote_verbatim: we have a framework where you can drop your own code into the fpga because all of our fpga code is open source
claims.speaker: Derek Kozel
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Derek Kozel

claims.claim_text: A soft microcontroller in fabric can be given exactly the peripheral complement a design needs, including an arbitrary number of serial ports, and each port can be paired with dedicated logic that polls its sensor and deposits the result in a register, removing the periodic servicing that would otherwise consume processor time.
claims.quote_verbatim: if you use an FPGA board, you can implement a soft microcontroller on it. And you can specify exactly how many serial ports you want.
claims.speaker: Luke Valenty
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Luke Valenty

claims.claim_text: The fine-pitch BGA packages that hold the smallest capable FPGAs are specified for high-density interconnect processes: via-in-pad with 0.2 mm vias on a 0.1 mm drill, filled and plated, which puts prototype fabrication into the thousands of dollars.
claims.quote_verbatim: the official recommendation is to use via in pad with, you know, 0.2 millimeter vias and like a 0.1 millimeter drill
claims.speaker: Luke Valenty
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Luke Valenty

claims.claim_text: Unused FPGA I/O pins default to tri-state, which makes it safe to route signal traces across their unused pads under solder mask in order to escape a dense package — a technique that fails only if a user later drives those pins deliberately.
claims.quote_verbatim: on an FPGA, if you don't use a pin, one of the IO pins, um, in almost all cases, it'll be tri-stated by default
claims.speaker: Luke Valenty
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Luke Valenty

claims.claim_text: The open-source iCE40 toolchain is small enough to be hosted on a server or run inside a web browser, which collapses the path from plugging in a board to a blinking LED to a matter of minutes.
claims.quote_verbatim: with the Ice Storm tools, you could host that on your cloud servers or you could even conceivably, you know, put that and run it within the web browser itself
claims.speaker: Luke Valenty
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Luke Valenty

claims.claim_text: The low-cost software-defined instrument category is architecturally an FPGA behind an analogue front end, with the host software defining which instrument the box currently is; the fabric supplies the speed and logic handling that a microcontroller could not.
claims.quote_verbatim: this Analog Discovery 2 I have is basically an FPGA with front end on it
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: The Synergy Bus

claims.claim_text: 100 Mbit Ethernet cannot be probed directly with an oscilloscope because the line encoding makes traffic indistinguishable from noise and gives no usable trigger; the practical instrument is an Ethernet PHY that provides a data-valid signal, followed by a small FPGA that parallelises the data into a scope's parallel bus for decoding.
claims.quote_verbatim: With like 100 meg Ethernet, you can't just stick a scope on the line because it looks like noise because of the encoding.
claims.speaker: Mike Harrison
claims.episode_title: 3 Cent Micros And 1000s of LEDs

claims.claim_text: The FPGA market has long consisted of four established vendors: Altera, absorbed into Intel; Xilinx; Lattice; and Microsemi, formerly Actel, whose families include PolarFire.
claims.quote_verbatim: So there's four microcontroller. Oh. Or sorry, FPGA vendors. There's Altera slash Intel at Xilinx. There's Lattice. And then there's Micro Semi. They used to be Actel.
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: Feels over reals

claims.claim_text: A first FPGA project should be something a microcontroller cannot do easily — heavily parallel work, real-time serial decoding, or building a processor from scratch — since blinking an LED demonstrates nothing about the fabric; running a vendor demo is worthwhile only as toolchain familiarisation.
claims.quote_verbatim: Like it's, it's pointless to flash a lead. I think if you're going to go to FPGA, you need something that, you know, is not really easily doable on a microcontroller.
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Feels over reals

claims.claim_text: The Lattice ECP5 evaluation board, at 100 dollars and 85,000 logic elements, was the largest FPGA with usable open-source tool support, making it the practical ceiling for open-toolchain work.
claims.quote_verbatim: There's the ECP5 evaluation board for $100, which is a very good place to start. That's an 85,000 logic element FPGA.
claims.speaker: David Shah
claims.episode_title: Open FPGA Toolchains at 35c3

claims.claim_text: RISC-V displaced ad-hoc and legacy architectures as the default soft-core target because its compiler support in GCC, Clang and LLVM improved rapidly, which matters more than gate count when the core has to be handed to end users.
claims.quote_verbatim: RISC-V is a much, much better target and has very, very rapidly improving compiler support in GCC and Clang and LLVM
claims.speaker: Claire Wolf
claims.episode_title: Open FPGA Toolchains at 35c3

claims.claim_text: A 32-bit RISC-V core fits in roughly half of a 5,000 logic element iCE40 part, leaving the other half for custom peripherals; soft-core competitions demonstrated how far that footprint can be squeezed.
claims.quote_verbatim: the Icebreaker board, for example, has a fairly small FPGA, about 5,000 logic elements. But nevertheless, if you want to build a 32-bit processor for it, it maybe takes up half of the space.
claims.speaker: Claire Wolf
claims.episode_title: Open FPGA Toolchains at 35c3

claims.claim_text: Yosys, a recursive acronym for the Yosys Open SYnthesis Suite, is the synthesis stage of the open-source FPGA flow, which is completed by separate place-and-route and bitstream-packing tools.
claims.quote_verbatim: So it's Yosis Open Synthesis Suite.
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: Pulled From A Working Environment

claims.claim_text: The open-source FPGA flow completes synthesis, place and route in around twenty seconds for a design whose vendor flow took about eight minutes, and that iteration speed changes how the tool is used rather than merely saving time.
claims.quote_verbatim: you click go and it's like 20 seconds, Dave. It's insane. And like, and like they actually timed it. They said it would have been an eight minute.
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: Pulled From A Working Environment

claims.claim_text: Wishbone is a standardised on-chip bus used inside FPGAs to attach custom peripherals to a soft CPU; because the bus is addressable from outside through a host bridge, a running program's peripheral state can be altered directly rather than by patching its code.
claims.quote_verbatim: that's like a way to, like a standardized bus in FPGA is to like add peripherals to a microcontroller, a soft, uh, soft CPU that might be in there
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: Pulled From A Working Environment

claims.claim_text: Through the early 2000s the overwhelming majority of both Xilinx and Altera revenue came from telecommunications, with military and aerospace as secondary segments, which left the FPGA vendors directly exposed to the telecoms downturn after the dot-com collapse.
claims.quote_verbatim: an overwhelming majority of Xilinx and, indeed, Altera's revenue came from the telecommunications market
claims.speaker: Kieran O'Leary
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Kieran O'Leary

claims.claim_text: Integration of hard intellectual property alongside FPGA fabric began in the early 2000s with the PowerPC embedded in the Xilinx Virtex-II Pro and the arrival of the MicroBlaze soft core; a large array of lookup tables alone had ceased to be enough.
claims.quote_verbatim: the PowerPC embedded in the Vertex 2 Pro
claims.speaker: Kieran O'Leary
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Kieran O'Leary

claims.claim_text: A Chinese-vendor FPGA with 1,152 lookup tables, 864 flip-flops and 72 kilobits of block SRAM appeared on complete five-dollar development boards, well below the price point of the four established vendors' entry parts.
claims.quote_verbatim: It's got 1,152 LUTs, 864 flip-flops, 72K a block SRAM.
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: KonnectorPanik

claims.claim_text: PYNQ is a Python framework for Zynq FPGA system-on-chip parts, used mainly in education because it lowers the barrier to entry for courses that cannot spend twelve weeks building a Linux system on custom hardware from the transistor up.
claims.quote_verbatim: It's like P it's like zinc Z Y N Q, but with a P P O N Q. That's it's like a Python for FPGAs generally speaking.
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Ryan Cousins

claims.claim_text: Contrary to the reputation for high power draw, an FPGA can be orders of magnitude more computationally efficient than a CPU or GPU for a suitable workload, because the algorithm itself is laid out in parallel rather than replicated across many cores that still execute sequentially.
claims.quote_verbatim: FPGAs are actually like orders of magnitude, uh, or can be orders of magnitude more computationally efficient than something like a CPU or GPU
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Ryan Cousins

claims.claim_text: Modern FPGA fabric provides no internal tri-state buffers, so the single bidirectional bus of classic microprocessor systems cannot be reproduced; an on-chip bus is instead built as two unidirectional buses, one from master to peripherals and one gathering peripheral outputs through a multiplexer back to the master.
claims.quote_verbatim: in order to make that work, you need two buses. Like, in one bus from the master to all the peripherals, and then from all the peripherals, there's like a separate bus that goes into a multiplexer that goes back into the master.
claims.speaker: Jeroen Domburg
claims.episode_title: Stories from Supercon 2019

claims.claim_text: Verilog is the more practical first hardware description language despite a steep learning curve, because the open-source tools favour it and most published cores and examples are written in it; VHDL remains common but narrows the available toolchain.
claims.quote_verbatim: I tend to lean toward Verilog because, uh, most of the open source tools, um, use Verilog more than VHDL
claims.speaker: Sylvain Minot
claims.episode_title: Stories from Supercon 2019

claims.claim_text: Learning to simulate before targeting hardware is standard advice for FPGA beginners, with Icarus Verilog and Verilator as the open-source simulators in common use.
claims.quote_verbatim: that's actually the other thing that I would recommend for people is to learn to simulate first
claims.speaker: Sylvain Minot
claims.episode_title: Stories from Supercon 2019

claims.claim_text: By the late 2010s a 12,000 lookup-table FPGA cost five or six dollars in modest quantities, enough to host a soft processor, but still without a cost case against a microcontroller for anything other than future-proofing.
claims.quote_verbatim: the one that's, like, 12,000 is, like, $5, $6, you know, at decently low quantities
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: The Tiny Lab Movement

claims.claim_text: Length matching to a large FPGA has to account for two effects beyond trace length: propagation delay differs by layer, so skew must be computed per net from per-layer lengths, and the package itself contributes an on-die delay before the signal reaches the BGA ball.
claims.quote_verbatim: these FPGA parts are so big, they actually have a delay on chip, too, before the signal gets to the BGA
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Craig J Bishop

claims.claim_text: Verilog is increasingly treated as the assembly language of FPGA design, generated by higher-level Python-based tools such as MyHDL, Migen and LiteX; it still has to be understood for debugging what those generators emit.
claims.quote_verbatim: I think Verilog is becoming like the assembly language of FPGAs and stuff. So that way we don't directly deal with it most of the time, but you want to know it for debugging
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Craig J Bishop

claims.claim_text: Clock-domain crossing is hard to implement correctly by hand and produces subtle, intermittent FPGA failures, so it should be taken from a standard library primitive; awkward clock ratios such as 33 to 50 MHz make hand-rolled solutions worse.
claims.quote_verbatim: There's a clock domain crossing standard library primitives. Oh, yeah. Which is really hard to get right. Otherwise, in FPGA, there's kind of subtle problems.
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Craig J Bishop

claims.claim_text: An image sensor can be run in a one-bit serial mode in which the FPGA supplies the clock and receives a data bit plus frame and line sync pulses, reconstructing the image in fabric; this is how a full camera interface is fitted through only two spare I/O pins.
claims.quote_verbatim: the camera outputs a data stream over a single bit. So you send it a clock and it will send back a data value, a frame sync and a line sync pulse. And then the FPGA can interpret all these signals and reconstruct the image.
claims.speaker: Greg Davill
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Greg Davill

claims.claim_text: An FPGA drawing large current surges at power-up drives a bulk capacitance requirement distinct from the high-frequency decoupling needed during operation, and each chip on a board has its own bypass profile determined by switching speed, layout and function.
claims.quote_verbatim: if it's an fpga that draws massive gulps of current when it first powers on you know you might need a lot of bulk capacitance
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Sowing Discord

claims.claim_text: Radiation-induced upsets in an FPGA's configuration can be cleared by reconfiguring the affected region, which turns a radiation-tolerance problem into a computer-architecture problem of detecting and recovering from bit flips rather than a physics problem.
claims.quote_verbatim: reconfiguring the hardware can actually flush out faults that may have been caused by radiation in space
claims.speaker: Brock Lameres
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Brock LaMeres

claims.claim_text: A radiation-tolerant computer can be built by instantiating redundant processor cores in one FPGA and voting on their outputs, so a core corrupted by radiation is outvoted; the recovery step reconfigures the faulted core and reintroduces it to the voting set.
claims.quote_verbatim: the idea is to basically take a FPGA and put redundant processing cores on it and then vote on the output
claims.speaker: Brock Lameres
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Brock LaMeres

claims.claim_text: Packaging an FPGA as a chiplet adds a layer of post-fabrication customisability inside a multi-die package, letting a custom part combine RF, power and fixed logic dies with a region that remains reprogrammable for years.
claims.quote_verbatim: FPGA as a chiplet, it gives you one more layer of customizability on top of the smart fabric programmability.
claims.speaker: Ming Zhang
claims.episode_title: Discussing Chiplets with Ming Zhang

claims.claim_text: The attraction of FPGAs for large infrastructure operators is a software-style deployment cycle — a change reaching hardware worldwide in minutes rather than years — bought at a substantial silicon and power cost for the configurability itself.
claims.quote_verbatim: FPGAs give a software style deployment, I can deploy worldwide in, you know, minutes instead of years. Um, and the thing is though, that FPGAs pay a pretty high cost for that configurability.
claims.speaker: Tim Ansell
claims.episode_title: Discussing the Open Source PDK with Tim Ansell

claims.claim_text: Open process design kits made it possible to fabricate an FPGA itself as an open design, with a University of Utah project targeting the SkyWater process.
claims.quote_verbatim: a project called open FPGA, um, that's done out of the university of Utah, um, that is trying to build a, uh, open FPGA on the skywater process
claims.speaker: Tim Ansell
claims.episode_title: Discussing the Open Source PDK with Tim Ansell

claims.claim_text: FPGAs offer two kinds of on-chip memory: small amounts distributed within the logic cells, and dedicated block RAM instantiated explicitly. The split and the block sizes are vendor-specific, so memory structure is one of the least portable parts of a design.
claims.quote_verbatim: then there's also block RAM that you can access
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: Fabless Chip Design with Mohamed Kassem

claims.claim_text: In the mid-1990s entry into programmable logic cost thousands of dollars at minimum, with the design software alone running into thousands before any silicon, which is why the field was closed to individuals until low-cost boards and free tool tiers appeared.
claims.quote_verbatim: Back when FPGAs were like getting into FPGAs or programmable logic was thousands of dollars minimum
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: This Is Just A Tribute

claims.claim_text: Cheap entry-level programmable logic tool packages were deliberately made file-incompatible with the vendor's professional tools, so a design started in the low-cost environment could not be carried upward and had to be re-entered.
claims.quote_verbatim: They stripped down their software and deliberately made it not compatible with their main tools
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: This Is Just A Tribute

claims.claim_text: CPLDs and older programmable logic devices use a fundamentally different fabric from FPGAs — a fixed product-term array rather than lookup tables and a routing network — which is why they behave differently on timing and configuration.
claims.quote_verbatim: Programmable logic devices have essentially a fundamentally different fabric to FPGAs.
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: This Is Just A Tribute

claims.claim_text: Where a platform must track a moving workload, such as evolving machine-learning models, an FPGA lets the hardware change with a new bitstream instead of a new tape-out; the usual progression is to prototype and iterate in fabric and move to custom silicon only when the design and the volume have both settled.
claims.quote_verbatim: You don't have to, like, tape out a new chip. You just kind of push a new bitstream onto it.
claims.speaker: Michael Gielda
claims.episode_title: Simulating Embedded Hardware with Michael Gielda

claims.claim_text: Distributed real-time installations can be synchronised by having each node's FPGA run a free-running 48 MHz 64-bit counter as its master time base and report it to a central computer over UDP, which then profiles each node's clock against its own rather than trying to force them into lockstep.
claims.quote_verbatim: the FPGA basically ran a 48 meg 64-bit counter as its master timing value
claims.speaker: Daryl Tewksbury
claims.episode_title: Outdoor Laser Projection & Object Mapping with Daryl Tewksbury

claims.claim_text: A CPLD is preferred over an FPGA where the design is small, the pin count must be low, and timing must be predictable: FPGA routing is less deterministic than the CPLD's fixed interconnect, even though the FPGA is far faster in absolute terms.
claims.quote_verbatim: you want better timing and stuff like that because the FPGAs, their routing's a bit more loosey goosey than the, uh, let's just say than the CPLDs
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: LEDs and EVs with Mike Harrison

claims.claim_text: The FPGA market splits by power envelope: data-centre parts demand the newest process nodes, where mask sets alone cost millions of dollars, so only the largest vendors compete there, while edge and battery-powered applications are served by lower-density, low-power fabrics on older nodes.
claims.quote_verbatim: in those markets, you really have to chase the process technology curve
claims.speaker: Brian Faith
claims.episode_title: Open FPGA Toolchains and Machine Learning with Brian Faith of QuickLogic

claims.claim_text: An embedded FPGA, or eFPGA, is a block of reconfigurable fabric included as one core among many inside a larger system-on-chip, as distinct from a discrete FPGA where the fabric is the whole device.
claims.quote_verbatim: So EFPGA is embedded FPGA. So if there's a FPGA core in a bigger processor, we typically would call that an EFPGA.
claims.speaker: Brian Faith
claims.episode_title: Open FPGA Toolchains and Machine Learning with Brian Faith of QuickLogic

claims.claim_text: Logic cell counts are not comparable between vendors because the cells differ in what they can absorb, so a capacity figure is only meaningful as a range or against a specific design.
claims.quote_verbatim: different logic cells have different utilization, depending on who, which competitor you're talking about
claims.speaker: Brian Faith
claims.episode_title: Open FPGA Toolchains and Machine Learning with Brian Faith of QuickLogic

claims.claim_text: USB is normally treated as needing dedicated silicon and a licensed hard core, but a device-side USB core can be implemented in a small embedded FPGA fabric of one to two thousand logic cells, with the FPGA's own pins driving the connector.
claims.quote_verbatim: we've actually implemented a soft USB core in the FPGA, which is amazing. So that FPGA, the FPGA pins are what's driving that USB connector on Quickfeather, not a USB hard core.
claims.speaker: Brian Faith
claims.episode_title: Open FPGA Toolchains and Machine Learning with Brian Faith of QuickLogic

claims.claim_text: In an auto-ranging current meter the range switch must complete before the burden voltage across the sense resistor collapses the supply to the device under test; a target jumping from microamps to an amp in under 100 microseconds forces a range decision in about a microsecond, which is why the ranging logic sits in an FPGA rather than a microcontroller.
claims.quote_verbatim: if you don't react quickly, will cause a voltage drop, burden voltage, over the sense resistor inside Julescope. And if it gets too big, it would brown out your device.
claims.speaker: Matt Liberty
claims.episode_title: Measuring Current with Matt Liberty

claims.claim_text: Keeping two external analogue-to-digital converters exactly in sample-time synchronisation is difficult with a microcontroller and straightforward in fabric, which is a common reason for an FPGA in an instrument front end.
claims.quote_verbatim: So, the FPGA there is running the ADC. So, I have two external ADCs, and it keeps them completely in sync
claims.speaker: Matt Liberty
claims.episode_title: Measuring Current with Matt Liberty

claims.claim_text: Embedding FPGA fabric in a microcontroller carries high area and power overhead and a steep learning curve, which is why the RP2040 instead provides programmable I/O blocks: stripped-down programmable state machines specialised to serial I/O with the area and power cost of an ordinary serial peripheral, able to implement VGA, I2S, SD card and DVI interfaces.
claims.quote_verbatim: you can have things like FPGAs on board your microcontroller, but they have a high area and power overhead. And they tend to be quite a steep learning curve to program for software engineers.
claims.speaker: Luke Renn
claims.episode_title: Embedded Hardware with the Raspberry Pi Team

claims.claim_text: A programmable I/O block is not a small FPGA: it lacks a general routing fabric, so logic is confined to the I/O pins it serves and cannot be arbitrarily interconnected.
claims.quote_verbatim: It doesn't have the routability. Yeah. So it's not like a true FPGA. It's more like a, I think it's like a configurable logic machine that's on these IO pins.
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: Trade Show or Conference?

claims.claim_text: Efinix was founded in late 2012 by former Altera engineers who judged a full FPGA business impossible to build from scratch, and planned instead to develop the technology, license it, and be acquired; a team of under ten people produced the software and early prototype devices before the company shifted to selling its own products from 2017.
claims.quote_verbatim: our original goal was really try to build a technology technology and work on a few licensed possibilities and expect it we will get acquired within a short period of time
claims.speaker: Sammy Cheung
claims.episode_title: Efinix FPGAs with Sammy Cheung

claims.claim_text: Intel's 2015 acquisition of Altera reframed the FPGA from a general-purpose logic device into data-centre and data-processing infrastructure, and in doing so removed the prospective acquirers that smaller programmable-logic companies had been counting on.
claims.quote_verbatim: It was very clear that FPGA wasn't just a general purpose logic device. It's being used in data center.
claims.speaker: Sammy Cheung
claims.episode_title: Efinix FPGAs with Sammy Cheung

claims.claim_text: A modern small FPGA is sold as three capabilities in one device: general-purpose custom logic, a reconfigurable neural network implementation, and low-latency data-path processing, with DSP and memory blocks designed to work with the routing architecture rather than bolted on.
claims.quote_verbatim: it's still an FPGA you can do general purpose custom logic on the other hand you can embed a reconfigurable neural net implementation and on the same chip you can do the data path low latency computing processing
claims.speaker: Sammy Cheung
claims.episode_title: Efinix FPGAs with Sammy Cheung

claims.claim_text: One vendor departed from the Vivado and Quartus tool model by separating the fabric core from its periphery in an interface designer, a distinct piece of software that configures the I/O and anything attached to the core, on the reasoning that the periphery is what varies between customers.
claims.quote_verbatim: our tools look different from standard FPGA because of the interface designer
claims.speaker: Sammy Cheung
claims.episode_title: Efinix FPGAs with Sammy Cheung

claims.claim_text: A multi-core Linux-capable system-on-chip built from open RISC-V cores such as VexRiscv fits in about 35,000 lookup tables or fewer, which is mid-range rather than high-end fabric.
claims.quote_verbatim: you can put a multi-core Linux capable SOC into your FPGA. And I'm not talking about like a huge VU19 FPGA. I'm talking about something that has, you know, 35K LUTs or less
claims.speaker: Michael Gielda
claims.episode_title: Open Source Mindset with Michael Gielda

claims.claim_text: Vendor IP cores bundled with a toolchain win on economics rather than merit: building the equivalent from open sources is roughly twice the work, so open alternatives only displace them where they are already good enough to use unchanged.
claims.quote_verbatim: building this from scratch is twice the work that just grabbing Silenx IP
claims.speaker: Michael Gielda
claims.episode_title: Open Source Mindset with Michael Gielda

claims.claim_text: The baseboard management controller in a server, conventionally a fixed ASIC, can be replaced by an FPGA carrying open-source cores and peripherals, which makes the management path inspectable and modifiable rather than an opaque piece of hard silicon with privileged access.
claims.quote_verbatim: what if you could just put an FPGA there and make it much more configurable and secure and transparent
claims.speaker: Michael Gielda
claims.episode_title: Open Source Mindset with Michael Gielda

claims.claim_text: Implementing a memory controller in FPGA fabric rather than using a fixed system-on-chip is what makes memory-attack research possible, since the access patterns that trigger a fault can be varied directly; this approach found new Rowhammer vulnerabilities in memories advertised as protected.
claims.quote_verbatim: being able to tweak your controller means that you can you know fiddle around with what kind of stuff triggers a problem much more easily
claims.speaker: Michael Gielda
claims.episode_title: Open Source Mindset with Michael Gielda

claims.claim_text: Most FPGA I/O is interchangeable, which lets a layout engineer reassign pins to simplify routing, but some pins are fixed by function or bank; a schematic handed to a separate layout engineer must flag which pins may not be swapped, or the constraint is silently violated.
claims.quote_verbatim: these pins are not swappable
claims.speaker: Shrouk El Attar
claims.episode_title: Creative Engineering with Shrouk El-Attar

claims.claim_text: An FPGA's internal input comparators can be combined with external passives to form an analogue-to-digital converter, removing a dedicated ADC from the bill of materials for undemanding measurements.
claims.quote_verbatim: I learned how to use the internal comparators of the FPGAs and sort of turn that into an ADC instead of having a separate ADC
claims.speaker: Shrouk El Attar
claims.episode_title: Creative Engineering with Shrouk El-Attar

claims.claim_text: The NanoBoard system identified attached peripheral modules by one-wire serial number and automatically pulled in the corresponding FPGA IP, giving genuine plug-and-play at the level of hardware blocks.
claims.quote_verbatim: you could actually plug in the modules and it'd auto detect them via one wire serial numbers and stuff. And then it'd pull in the FPGA stuff.
claims.speaker: Ben Jordan
claims.episode_title: Publicly Traded Hobby with Ben Jordan

claims.claim_text: The four-thousand-dollar FPGA development platform did not sell, and a roughly three-hundred-dollar successor sold well, an order-of-magnitude repricing that indicates where the market for such platforms actually sat.
claims.quote_verbatim: the $4,000 board didn't sell. So they eventually came out with a $300 version, which sold
claims.speaker: Ben Jordan
claims.episode_title: Publicly Traded Hobby with Ben Jordan

claims.claim_text: The bet that all designs would move inside FPGAs failed on cost and power. The exception proves the rule: the customers for whom the modular FPGA approach did work were makers of low-volume, high-value products such as medical devices, where non-recurring engineering dominates unit cost.
claims.quote_verbatim: it just didn't pan out because FPGAs are too expensive. They're too power hungry.
claims.speaker: Ben Jordan
claims.episode_title: Publicly Traded Hobby with Ben Jordan

claims.claim_text: The Fomu is an iCE40 UP5K FPGA board small enough to sit entirely inside a computer's USB port, with the fabric implementing the USB interface itself.
claims.quote_verbatim: it's an FPGA board, which is so small, it goes inside the USB port of a computer
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: Timing is Everything

claims.claim_text: FPGA power delivery changes character with device class: a low-end part drawing an amp or two is fed by an ordinary switching regulator, but the next tier drawing thirty to fifty amps requires a multiphase regulator, and top-end accelerator parts reach around 250 amps.
claims.quote_verbatim: We're used to using, you know, the low end FPGA that pulls an amp or two and, you know, you plop down your whatever jelly bean switcher and it works just fine. And all of a sudden they go up the next rung of the ladder and it pulls only 30 to 50 amps
claims.speaker: Carmen
claims.episode_title: Switching Converter Engineering with Carmen Parisi

claims.claim_text: Schematic entry survives in FPGA tools for a legitimate reason: consolidating discrete glue logic such as shift registers and flip-flops into one small FPGA does not justify learning a hardware description language.
claims.quote_verbatim: if you just got a simple design and you want to consolidate some glue, some, you know, logic, glue logic, right. Into one little FPGA that solves your little problem. You don't want to write hate, learn and write HDL for it.
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: The Rodeo Drive of Electronics

claims.claim_text: Optical and imaging systems reach for FPGAs and CPLDs because the sensors impose tight timing that a microcontroller could only meet with a substantially more powerful part and a real-time operating system, and because the same data then needs parallel processing.
claims.quote_verbatim: there are lots of good reasons in a, in a, in an optical environment why you'd want to use an FPGA, mainly because the sensors require really tight timing
claims.speaker: Leigh Brady
claims.episode_title: Siloed Engineering with Leigh Brady

claims.claim_text: Custom logic written into an FPGA comes with no datasheet: the designer is building on blocks that nobody has documented, which is a real cost in maintenance and in consulting work where the time is hard to bill.
claims.quote_verbatim: nobody wrote the data sheet for that custom lot that you wrote the logic and then you're building on top of that
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: Rebuilding Projects with Dave Young

claims.claim_text: The habits an FPGA designer brings to an ASIC mislead: on an FPGA every logic tile supplies a lookup table, a flip-flop and a carry chain whether or not they are used, whereas on an ASIC every element is placed deliberately and a flip-flop is six to eight times the area of an inverter.
claims.quote_verbatim: you're used to getting a flip-flop on every logic tile, but with an ASIC, that's not the case
claims.speaker: Matt Venn
claims.episode_title: Open Source Tapeout with Matthew Venn

claims.claim_text: A bring-up technique for a fabricated processor is to use an FPGA to model the memory the chip executes from, count the instructions retired, and sweep the core voltage to plot instructions executed against voltage, revealing the undervolted operating point at which enough of the design still functions.
claims.quote_verbatim: he made a really fancy system that used an FPGA to model the memory that the Pico RV32 RISC-V processor on the ASIC executed out of
claims.speaker: Matt Venn
claims.episode_title: Open Source Tapeout with Matthew Venn

claims.claim_text: The ability to reconfigure fabric and push field updates erodes the ASIC discipline of proving the architecture and test coverage before committing masks, since a mistake no longer has to be right the first time.
claims.quote_verbatim: nobody thinks like an ASIC designer anymore. Cause everything's FPGA. They can change it. They can push field updates
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Super Tecmo Bug

claims.claim_text: Reformatting acquired data into an audio stream in an FPGA lets a processor's serial audio interface be used as a high-throughput 32-bit sample transport, reusing a well-supported peripheral instead of building a custom capture path.
claims.quote_verbatim: this all gets mangled from the two ADCs into two FPGAs which turns it into audio signals for the IMX RT-1060 so I can use the the great serial audio interfaces on the IMX to retrieve all these 32-bit samples
claims.speaker: Werner Johansson
claims.episode_title: Software Defined Power Supplies with Werner Johansson

claims.claim_text: Custom chip development prototypes each controller as an FPGA build that exposes the PHY interface on FPGA pins, run on a commercial prototyping system whose daughter cards carry real PHYs and connectors, so the controller is proven against real physical layers while the ASIC PHY itself can only be simulated and trusted until first silicon.
claims.quote_verbatim: for RP1, we used a pro FPGA system. So that's, it sort of has loads of daughter cards
claims.speaker: Liam Fraser
claims.episode_title: The RP1 and beyond with the Raspberry Pi Hardware team

claims.claim_text: Verilog and VHDL are among the few genuinely universal hardware standards: RTL written without vendor-specific IP blocks can be pushed through different vendors' FPGA flows, and with care through an ASIC flow, unchanged. The languages are harder than Python, but that portability is what they buy.
claims.quote_verbatim: if I don't use IP blocks from a specific vendor, I can kind of push the button through and it just works. If I wrote the right RTL code and I can run that on a, you know, different vendors, FPGA devices
claims.speaker: Andreas Olofsson
claims.episode_title: Accessible ASICs with Andreas Olofsson

claims.claim_text: Intel moved its FPGA business back out as a separate entity after absorbing Altera, leaving the programmable-logic line independent again while remaining tied to Intel's foundry.
claims.quote_verbatim: FPGAs are still a profitable business, I'm sure, generally, but like, why do you need it to be part of Intel? I don't know. So they're moving it back out.
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: Altium...Acquired!

claims.claim_text: A roughly twenty-dollar Gowin 9K-class FPGA holds a complete 1990s-era computer including an MS-DOS-capable emulator with HDMI output, which is the practical measure of what an entry-level modern part contains.
claims.quote_verbatim: the GoWin FPGAs, like 20 bucks for the 9K. One is able to run MS-DOS emulator on that with HDMI output.
claims.speaker: Bitluni
claims.episode_title: Lifelong Learning with Bitluni

claims.claim_text: In satellite design the split between processors and FPGAs follows the interface load: the platform avionics use mostly processors, while payloads carry many FPGAs because they must interface to numerous different high-speed interfaces.
claims.quote_verbatim: We've got a lot of processors on board and not a lot of FPGAs, but the payloads have got a lot of FPGAs because they're interfacing to different, lots of different high-speed sort of interfaces.
claims.speaker: Dan Esparon
claims.episode_title: Satellite Design Engineering with Dan Esparon

claims.claim_text: A soft core running at only about 20 MHz can outperform expectations because the hardware around it is malleable: rearranging eight bits scattered across eight registers so that they sit in one register replaces sixteen read-and-mask instructions with a single read, an eightfold gain that has no equivalent on fixed silicon.
claims.quote_verbatim: if you need to read eight, you know, bits from eight different registers, you could rearrange that. So it's only one read
claims.speaker: Tim Ansell
claims.episode_title: Building wafer.space with Tim Ansell

claims.claim_text: Low-cost instrument makers have moved away from Xilinx Artix-7-class parts to substantially cheaper Chinese FPGAs, which alongside custom front-end ASICs and ADCs is what allows price points the established vendors cannot match.
claims.quote_verbatim: instead of using a Xilinx FPGA, which are quite expensive, right?
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Tugging on the Nerd Heartstring

claims.claim_text: Where a display or other peripheral uses a non-standard parallel bus, one solution is a dedicated FPGA whose entire function is protocol translation; the cost of that part disappears if a system-on-chip vendor integrates the same interface, which is a real selection criterion when choosing a chip.
claims.quote_verbatim: we actually put down an, an, a separate FPGA whose job it was solely to translate, you know, commands to this really weird bus system
claims.speaker: Eric Migicovsky
claims.episode_title: Shiny New Pebble with Eric Migicovsky

claims.claim_text: In an ASIC accelerator project the validated RTL is ported to an FPGA with wrappers mapping its I/O to the FPGA's pins, so the design can be exercised against real microcontroller firmware during the nine months the ASIC spends at the fab; hardening to the target process follows, with area and target-frequency closure checked continuously rather than at the end.
claims.quote_verbatim: it's going to take nine months for my ASIC to come back from the fab. So I want something that is usable now and that's where the FPGAs come in
claims.speaker: Julia Desmazes
claims.episode_title: Chip Design for Fun (and Waffles) with Julia Desmazes

claims.claim_text: Tcl is the scripting language that drives FPGA and ASIC tool flows, so build automation in this domain means writing Tcl regardless of which vendor's tools are in use.
claims.quote_verbatim: It's just like tickle. Everything's tickle.
claims.speaker: Julia Desmazes
claims.episode_title: Chip Design for Fun (and Waffles) with Julia Desmazes
